papers.what_it_is: A classical machine learning paper that trains a matrix-product-state (tensor-train) weight tensor over an exponentially large product feature map with a DMRG-style sweeping algorithm, and reports 0.97% test error on MNIST.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the largest MPS bond dimension tried, m = 120, a test error of 0.97% (97 misclassified images out of 10,000) was obtained after three sweeps, with a training set error of 0.05%, or 32 misclassified images.
quotes: The largest bond dimension we tried was m = 120, where after three sweeps we obtained a test error of 0.97% (97 misclassiﬁed images out of the test set of 10,000 images); the training set error was 0.05% or 32 misclassiﬁed images.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single empirical result on one data set, from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports one run per setting and no confidence interval or repeat over random seeds.

assertions.value: The authors report that for bond dimension m = 10 both the training and test error were about 5%, and for m = 20 the error dropped to only 2%.
quotes: For m = 10 we found both a training and test error of about 5%; for m = 20 the error dropped to only 2%.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single empirical result on one data set, from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that typically only two or three sweeps were needed to see good convergence on MNIST, with test error rates changing only hundredths of a percent thereafter.
quotes: Typically only two or three sweeps were needed to see good convergence, with test error rates changing only hundreths of a percent thereafter.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single empirical observation from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that MNIST images of 28 × 28 pixels were scaled down to 14 × 14 by averaging clusters of four pixels, with no other modification of the training or test sets, and that the calculations used the ITensor library.
quotes: Each image was originally 28 × 28 pixels, which we scaled down to 14×14 by averaging clusters of four pixels; otherwise we performed no further modiﬁcations to the training or test sets.
The calculations were implemented using the ITensor library [37].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup in Section VI.

assertions.value: The authors state that working with the smaller images reduced the training time, with the tradeoff that less information was available for learning.
quotes: Working with smaller images reduced the time needed for training, with the tradeoﬀ being that less information was available for learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its MNIST setup in Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not report a run on the full 28 × 28 images, so the size of the tradeoff is not measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that the MPS path orders the pixels in a zig-zag ordering, chosen so that on average spatially neighboring pixels stay as close to each other as possible along the one-dimensional path.
quotes: We chose a “zig-zag” ordering shown in Fig. 8, which on average keeps spatially neighboring pixels as close to each other as possible along the onedimensional MPS path.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup in Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: In Figure 8 the numbering runs left to right along each row (1 to 14, then 15 to 28), which is a row-by-row ordering rather than a snake that reverses direction on every other row.

assertions.value: The authors state that the scaling of the sweeping algorithm is d cubed times m cubed times N times N_L times N_T, where m is the MPS bond dimension, N the number of input components, N_L the number of labels and N_T the number of training inputs.
quotes: The scaling of the above algorithm is d3 m3 N NL NT , where recall m is the MPS bond dimension; N the number of input components; NL the number of labels; and NT the number of training inputs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement given without a derivation in the text; the exponent of d is the printed d3, read here as d cubed.

assertions.value: The authors state that advancing the projected inputs by one site after each SVD keeps the cost of each local step independent of the size of the input space, so the total algorithm scales only linearly with input space size.
quotes: This allows the cost of each local step of the algorithm to remain independent of the size of the input space, making the total algorithm scale only linearly with input space size.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement given without a formal derivation beyond the algorithm description.

assertions.value: The authors state that training the model scales linearly in the training set size and that the cost of evaluating an input is independent of the training set size.
quotes: Training the model scales linearly in the training set size; the cost for evaluating an input is independent of training set size.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in the introduction; the cost formula is given in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that in practice the cost is dominated by the large number of training inputs, and that their experiments blending stochastic gradient descent with MPS sweeping often reached single-digit classification errors but could not match the accuracy of the full gradient.
quotes: In practice, the cost is dominated by the large number of training inputs NT , so it would be very desirable to reduce this cost.
we could not match the accuracy of the full gradient.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limitation of its algorithm in Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: The stochastic-gradient experiments are not reported with numbers.

assertions.value: The authors state that keeping only the m largest singular values in the SVD of the bond tensor is guaranteed to produce an optimal approximation of that tensor, and that if all MPS tensors to the left and right are formed from possibly truncated unitary matrices, the optimality applies globally to the entire MPS.
quotes: Such a truncation is guaranteed to produce an optimal approximation of the tensor B
then the optimality of the truncation of B applies globally to the entire MPS as well
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without proof; the paper refers to Refs. 26 and 42 for background.
assertions.reader_inference: The local result is the standard Eckart-Young property of the SVD; the paper does not prove either statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that following the SVD of the improved bond tensor, the dimension of the new MPS bond can be chosen adaptively from the number of large singular values (defined by a threshold chosen in advance), so the MPS can be compressed by different amounts on each bond.
quotes: the dimension of the new MPS bond can be chosen adaptively based on number of large singular values (deﬁned by a threshold chosen in advance).
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the algorithm; the MNIST runs report a maximum bond dimension but no adaptive bond-dimension profile.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported MNIST results are given by the maximum bond dimension m, so the adaptive behavior is described but not shown with data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm varies only two neighboring MPS tensors at a time, which leads to a straightforward method for adaptively changing the MPS bond dimension, and that the cost function is the quadratic cost over the training inputs.
quotes: For concreteness, let us choose to optimize the quadratic cost
Our strategy for reducing this cost function will be to vary only two neighboring MPS tensors at a time within the approximation Eq. (5).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its own algorithm and cost function in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors define the feature map as a tensor product of one local feature map applied to each input component, with local dimension d and each local vector of unit norm, and for grayscale pixels with values between zero and one they use a simple local map built from a cosine and a sine of the pixel value.

Thus each xj is mapped to a ddimensional vector, which we require to have unit norm;

assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its feature map in Section II, Eqs. (2) and (3).

assertions.value: The authors state that the feature tensor is rank-1, a product state in physics terms, and that the full feature map can be viewed as a vector in a d to the power N dimensional space or an order-N tensor.
quotes: The full feature map Φ(x) can be viewed as a vector in a dN -dimensional space or as an order-N tensor.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the definition of the feature map in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that in machine learning terms the feature map defines a kernel that is the product of N local kernels, one for each component of the input, and that kernels of this type have been argued to be useful for data where no relationship is assumed between different components of the input vector prior to learning.
quotes: the feature map Eq. (2) deﬁnes a kernel which is the product of N local kernels, one for each component xj of the input data.
have been argued to be useful for data where no relationship is assumed between diﬀerent components of the input vector prior to learning [39].
assertions.certainty_reason: The usefulness claim is attributed to another reference.

assertions.value: The authors state that for multi-class learning they use a one-versus-all strategy with one weight vector per label, and classify an input by choosing the label for which the magnitude of the decision function is largest.
quotes: and classifying an input x by choosing the label for which |f (x)| is largest.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its classifier in Section III.

assertions.value: The authors state that the weight tensor has N_L times d to the power N components, where N_L is the number of labels, and that a tensor network approximates this exponentially large set of components with a much smaller set of parameters whose number grows only polynomially in the size of the input space.
quotes: A tensor network approximates the exponentially large set of components of a high-order tensor in terms of a much smaller set of parameters whose number grows only polynomially in the size of the input space.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about tensor networks in general; the number of parameters is not tabulated in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that for sufficiently large bond dimension m an MPS can represent any tensor, and that the bond dimension is the parameter controlling the MPS approximation.
quotes: For suﬃciently large m an MPS can represent any tensor [41].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to Ref. 41; no proof in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that a MERA network can explicitly model power-law decaying correlations while an MPS has exponentially decaying correlations, and that an MPS can still approximate power-law decays over quite long distances.
quotes: a MERA network can explicitly model power-law decaying correlations while a matrix product state (MPS) has exponentially decaying correlations [27].
Yet an MPS can still approximate power-law decays over quite long distances.
assertions.certainty_reason: The first statement is attributed to Ref. 27; the second is the authors' own statement without evidence in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that MPS are best suited to tensors with a one-dimensional pattern of correlations, but can also be a powerful approach for tensors with two-dimensional correlations.
quotes: Although MPS are best suited for approximating tensors with a one-dimensional pattern of correlations, they can also be a powerful approach for decomposing tensors with two-dimensional correlations as well [40].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to Ref. 40.

assertions.value: The authors state that in machine learning the bond dimension controls the number of parameters of the model, so taking too large a bond dimension might not be desirable as it could lead to overfitting, in contrast to physics where larger is better.
quotes: the bond dimension controls the number of parameters of the model.
taking too large a bond dimension might not be desirable as it could lead to overﬁtting.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement of expectation; the MNIST runs go up to m = 120 only.

assertions.value: The authors state that in typical physics applications the MPS bond dimension m can range from 10 to 10,000 or even more.
quotes: In typical physics applications the MPS bond dimension m can range from 10 to 10,000 or even more
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement of the authors without a citation.

assertions.value: The authors state that a related optimization algorithm for hidden Markov models in a cited reference uses a nonnegative matrix factorization in place of the SVD, and that where negative weights are allowed the SVD is the optimal choice because it minimizes the distance between the original tensor and the product of factorized tensors.
quotes: In a setting where negative weights are allowed, the SVD is the optimal choice because it minimizes the distance between the original tensor and product of factorized tensors.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without a proof in the paper.

popular interpretations of the hidden and output layers

papers.what_it_is: A survey and critique of quantum random access memory (QRAM) that argues active QRAM gives no asymptotic advantage over parallel classical computation for quantum linear algebra, proves a lower bound for circuit QRAM, and examines why passive hardware QRAM proposals fall short.

assertions.value: The authors state that linear-systems-based proposals promised to manipulate an N-dimensional vector in O(polylog N) time, and that an input stage costing Theta(N) against an algorithm costing polylog(N) is the entire runtime.
quotes: An input stage costing Θ(N ) against an algorithm costing polylog(N ) is not a constant-factor inconvenience; it is the entire runtime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the paper's Theta(N) claim for generic data.

assertions.value: The authors state that no QRAM device exists and that constructing one requires a hardware architecture qualitatively different from what is presently being built.
quotes: First, no such device exists, and constructing one requires a hardware architecture qualitatively different from what is presently being built.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author statement, attributed in part to Aaronson [6].

assertions.value: The authors state that a strong input model granting efficient superposition access to a structured dataset also grants efficient classical sampling access to the same structure, and that several headline exponential quantum machine learning speedups collapse to polynomial once the classical algorithm is granted comparable input access, citing Tang.
quotes: A strong input model granting efficient superposition access to a structured dataset also grants efficient classical sampling access to the same structure.

several headline exponential quantum machine learning speedups collapse to polynomial once the classical algorithm is granted input access comparable to what the quantum algorithm was assuming throughout.
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to Tang's dequantization results [7].

assertions.value: The authors describe a quantum kernel as estimating the squared overlap of feature states for pairs of data points, which requires preparing feature states for both points.
quotes: requiring the preparation of feature states for both.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of a quantum kernel in Section VI.

assertions.value: The authors state that wherever an advantage is claimed against classical data, the assumption made about introducing that data is load-bearing, and that it is usually contained in a sentence rather than a table.
quotes: Wherever an advantage is claimed against classical data, the assumption made about introducing that data is load-bearing
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement about the field; the paper reviews a few cases only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the input problem does not establish that quantum machine learning is futile, but that one argument pattern (classical dataset in, polylogarithmic quantum algorithm, exponential advantage out) does not close.
quotes: The input problem does not establish that quantum machine learning is futile.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its claim in Section VII.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the distribution is the output of a Hamiltonian simulation, a chemistry calculation or a variationally trained circuit, it was never a classical vector and there is nothing to load, and call this the cleanest escape.
quotes: it was never a classical vector and there is nothing to load.
This is the cleanest escape
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what its bound does not cover (Section VII).

assertions.value: The authors state that a shallow circuit trained to approximate a distribution avoids the Theta(N) angle count, and that whether the approximation suffices for a given downstream task is an open question.
quotes: Whether the approximation suffices for a given downstream task is an open and worthwhile question.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open problem in Section VII.

assertions.value: The authors state that if a single loaded state is consumed by many independent measurements the preparation cost divides, and that whether it divides sufficiently is an arithmetic question for any particular pipeline.
quotes: If a single loaded state is consumed by many independent measurements, the preparation cost divides.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what remains intact (Section VII).

assertions.value: The authors state that nothing in the paper forbids polynomial advantages, and that what is forbidden is an exponential advantage on generic classical input.
quotes: Nothing here forbids them. What is forbidden is an exponential advantage on generic classical input.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its claim (Section VII).

assertions.value: The authors report that a control experiment, transpiling the alternative, counting the same quantities and placing both in one table, took an afternoon and inverted the conclusion; they say every construction was verified against a closed-form answer to fourteen or more significant figures.
quotes: Each was verified against a closed-form answer to fourteen or more significant figures.
That experiment required an afternoon and it inverted the conclusion.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's own report of one study's experience.

assertions.value: The authors propose six questions to apply before any input-dependent advantage claim: how many numbers are computed classically before the circuit exists; whether gate counts were taken after transpilation; whether the method was benchmarked against the library implementation; whether it was benchmarked against the classical algorithm; whether state error, discretization error and shot noise are reported separately; and what the query costs if the speedup is stated in query complexity.
quotes: We therefore propose six questions to be applied before any input-dependent advantage claim, whether one’s own or another’s:
6. If the speedup is stated in query complexity, what does the query cost?
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its checklist in Section VIII.

assertions.value: The authors state that state error, discretization error and shot noise routinely differ by ten orders of magnitude, and that typically only the smallest is quoted.
quotes: They routinely differ by ten orders of magnitude, and typically only the smallest is quoted.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author statement from experience; no data in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that applied to the literature, most papers address two of the six questions.
quotes: Applied to the literature, most papers address two of the six.
assertions.certainty_reason: No survey, sample or count of papers is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that five executable Jupyter notebooks reproduce every construction and measurement, verified against Qiskit 2.5.1 and qiskit-aer 0.17.2, with each numerical result checked against a closed-form answer.
quotes: Five executable Jupyter notebooks reproduce every construction and measurement reported here, verified against Qiskit 2.5.1 and qiskit-aer 0.17.2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its software setup in the Code Availability section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the permanence of the input problem is not grounds for pessimism but for precision about which claims a given architecture can support.
quotes: This is not grounds for pessimism. It is grounds for precision about which claims a given architecture can support.
assertions.certainty_reason: A concluding opinion of the author.
